title: Session and token authority across issuance, verification, and revocation

threat_model.actor: Any caller who can present, plant, or forge a session identifier or bearer token, including a legitimate holder of an expired or revoked one
threat_model.asset: The authority a session or token confers: the subject it names, the scopes it carries, and the period for which it is honoured
threat_model.trust_boundary: The token as presented and the authority the verifier grants after reading it
threat_model.failure_mode: The verifier lets the token choose how it is verified, or the authority outlives the record that was supposed to govern it
threat_model.impact: A caller obtains or retains a session they were never granted or that was explicitly revoked, with the scopes attached to it

required_evidence: The application issues a session identifier or token that a later request presents to establish identity
A verification step exists between the presented value and the authority granted from it

signals: The algorithm is read from the token header rather than pinned by the verifier
One key map serves both symmetric and asymmetric verification, so a public key can be reached as a MAC secret
Claim checks are conditional on the claim being present, so an omitted exp, aud, or iss skips its check
A decode helper that does not verify is used somewhere on the request path
A resolved principal is cached in process, in a sidecar, or at a CDN edge without an invalidation path
Global revocation deletes the stored rows but does not reach derived state held by each worker
The identifier issued before authentication is promoted in place rather than rotated on privilege change
Scopes are read from the token but the resource check compares only the subject
A refresh exchange widens scopes or extends lifetime beyond the original grant
Downstream services accept a token minted for a different audience
A verifier selects the signature algorithm from the token header and the key from a mixed key map
A gateway caches resolved principals in process while global revocation only deletes stored rows

boundary.subject: the principal and scopes a presented token is allowed to assert
boundary.object: the authority the request executes with after verification
boundary.invariant: Authority is granted only from a token the verifier independently validated under its own pinned rules, and it ends when the governing record ends

examples: Signature check on a bearer token
Header-derived identity at a trusted proxy
Audience check before a downstream call
Global sign-out after a credential change

signals: Find every place a token is decoded and separate the decoding helpers from the verifying ones
Record where the algorithm, key, issuer, and audience come from, and whether any of them can be influenced by the token itself
Trace the resolved principal forward and note every cache, memo, or context object that stores it beyond the request
State which claims are mandatory and compare that with the checks the verifier performs unconditionally
Follow every revocation path to the state it must invalidate, including state held by other processes
Decide whether the identifier is rotated at every privilege change, not only at login
Establish the token lifetime, the revocation propagation delay, and what the gap between them permits
Identify long-lived artefacts that outlive the session: refresh tokens, API keys, device trust records
Present tokens with a substituted algorithm, an unknown key id, and omitted claims to the verifier in isolation and record which are accepted
Revoke a session and replay the same request against every process and cache tier that serves it

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and work only with synthetic accounts and locally generated keys
Establish a working authenticated control request first, so a later denial is distinguishable from a broken harness
Exercise the verification function in isolation with algorithm, key-id, and claim variants, and record exactly which inputs it accepts
Revoke the session through each documented revocation path and replay the control request against every serving tier
Record the verification point, the caching tiers, and the observed revocation delay without touching production credentials

false_positive_filters: The algorithm and key are pinned by the verifier and the token header is compared against them rather than consulted
The library in use rejects algorithm substitution by default and the configuration has been read rather than assumed
The cache is keyed and invalidated on every revocation path, evidenced in code rather than inferred from a comment
The token lifetime is short enough that the documented revocation model is stated as eventual and accepted with a rationale
The identifier is rotated at every privilege transition, so a planted value cannot become authenticated

required_evidence: The exact input the verifier accepts and the authority it grants for it
A reachable path from a caller-controlled token to the protected operation
A safe local reproduction that distinguishes a verification weakness from a key-management weakness
The defective invariant stated as a verification, rotation, or revocation failure, with its concrete authority impact
refutation_tests: Exercise the verifier alone on the same inputs to separate a parsing weakness from a request-time weakness
Re-read the library configuration for a pinned algorithm list before concluding the header is trusted
Check every revocation path for cache invalidation before concluding revoked authority persists
Establish whether the claimed key material is actually reachable by the attacker, since alg confusion needs a published key to matter

root_causes: The verifier lets the token select its own verification algorithm
Symmetric secrets and asymmetric public keys share one lookup, so a public value can act as a secret
Claim validation is conditional on presence, so omitting a claim omits its check
A pre-authentication identifier is promoted in place instead of rotated at the privilege transition
Authority is derived once and cached, while revocation only updates the source record
Scopes are read but never compared against the operation being performed

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Pin the algorithm, key, issuer, and audience in the verifier, require every security-relevant claim, and let revocation reach every tier that can grant authority
patterns: Reject any token whose header does not match the single expected algorithm, and keep symmetric and asymmetric keys in separate stores
Require exp, iat, iss, aud, and sub rather than checking them only when present
Rotate the session identifier at every privilege transition and destroy the previous one
Prefer an authoritative lookup per request over a cached decision, or bind every cache entry to an invalidation event and a short ceiling
Make global revocation reach derived state in every process, edge, and sidecar that can answer a request
Compare the token's scopes and audience against the operation, not only its subject

assertions: The vulnerable verifier accepts a token whose header selects a different algorithm from the one the issuer signed with
The vulnerable verifier accepts a token that omits the expiry claim entirely
The remediated verifier pins the algorithm, requires every security-relevant claim, and still accepts a correctly issued token
The vulnerable gateway keeps resolving a session that global revocation deleted, because the cached principal is never invalidated
The compensated gateway performs no explicit revocation check yet denies immediately after revocation, because the stored row is read on every request

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: Library defaults change between versions, so a verifier that looks permissive may be constrained by the version actually installed
Revocation behaviour depends on deployment topology: caches, edges, and sidecars outside the repository often decide the real delay
Fixtures demonstrate the verification contract, not the entropy or storage of production key material
A short token lifetime can be a deliberate, documented trade-off rather than a defect, and must be judged against the stated model
